newsitem.title: USA: Stocks break records, bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: Stocks break records, bonds rally.

text.p: Stocks broke more records and bonds rallied Friday as a surprisingly weak September jobs report eased fears of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
Investor demand for U.S. securities pushed up the dollar.

The Dow Jones industrial average rallied 60.01 points, or 1.01 percent, to a record closing high of 5,992.86 after hitting 5,995.47 earlier. That topped Wednesday's record close of 5,933.97. For the week, the blue chip index was up 119.94 points, or 2 percent.

"We're nearing my 1996 target of 6,100 and I think the stock market is headed higher than that. This remarkable rise is going to continue well into 1997 at least," said William LeFevre, a senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
In the broader market, advancing issues outpaced declines by 1,781 to 694 on very heavy volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks cruised through the 700 barrier, surging 8.68 points, or 1.25 percent, to 701.46 and topping Wednesday's record of 694.01. The index has scored record closes four times this week, ending up 15.27 from last Friday.
Likewise, the NYSE Composite index, which scored a record every day this week except Thursday, rose 4.02 to 374.16, an all-time high finish. The index was up 7.89 on the week.
The technology-studded Nasdaq Composite index soared 14.47 points, or 1.17 percent, to 1,247.56, just shy of June 5's record 1,249.15. The index was up 17.51 on the week.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond soared more than a full point, knocking its yield down to 6.75 percent from 6.84 percent at Thursday's close.
Stocks and bonds surged after the government said September non-farm payrolls fell 40,000, sharply weaker than the rise of 166,000 forecast by private economists and August's 241,000 increase.

While analysts deemed the report "one-way good news for bonds," it could prove to be a double-edged sword for stocks if moderating economic growth restrains corporate profit growth, said David Shulman, Salomon's chief equity strategist. "It raises questions for fourth-quarter earnings."

Shulman said investors were "coming to grips with a single-digit earnings growth environment," seeking out the technology, defensive and interest-rate sensitive issues that might outperform the broader market.

Several analysts expressed concern that a weaker economy would erode corporate profits in this sixth year of the bull market, the most powerful in history. But LeFevre, who started working on Wall Street when the Dow was at 160, was optimistic.
After earlier declines, the dollar rose to 1.5323 German marks in late New York trading from 1.5310 marks late Thursday, and to 111.79 Japanese yen from 111.47 yen.

Soybean prices fell as farmers were expected to make the season's first major harvest assault this weekend. Chicago Board of Trade November soybeans closed down 10-1/4 cents, a third of the daily 30-cent limit, at $7.27-1/4 per bushel, the lowest close since July 26.

Cocoa at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange ended higher bolstered by a strong European third quarter usage, market sources said. Benchmark CSCE December cocoa rose $9 a metric ton to $1,351.

Heating oil closed lower at the New York Mercantile Exchange, ending consecutive sessions of strong gains. As they did on the way up, crude oil and gasoline followed heating oil back down, traders said.

Heating oil for November delivery ended Friday 0.26 cent lower at 74.43 cents a gallon. Crude oil for November delivery dropped 8 cents to $24.73 a barrel and November gasoline fell 0.05 cent at 63.63 cents a gallon.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index set an intraday high of 4,025.1 points before ending at a record finish of 4,024.8, up 24.8 points on the day and 60.7 for the week. In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei 225 index slid 183.47 points or 0.86 percent to close at 21,148.03 but showed a rise of 35.79 on the week.
